title: Act III, Scene IV
focus: Capulet sets the wedding to Paris

teacherSummary.text: Late at night Capulet tells Paris that Juliet will marry him on Thursday, assuming her obedience.

vocabulary.context:
I will, and know her mind early to-morrow;
To-night she is mew’d up to her heaviness.
vocabulary.source: Liber et Libri contextual definition, hand-written against the line in Romeo and Juliet (2026-10-20)

etymology.text: “heaviness”: From Middle English hevynesse, from Old English hefiġnes "heaviness". Equivalent to heavy + -ness.
etymology.checked: 2026-10-20 (transcribed from the Wiktionary Etymology section; templates rendered, nothing added)

vocabulary.context:
We’ll keep no great ado—a friend or two;
For, hark you, Tybalt being slain so late,
It may be thought we held him carelessly,
Being our kinsman, if we revel much:
Therefore we’ll have some half a dozen friends,
And there an end.
vocabulary.source: Liber et Libri contextual definition, hand-written against the line in Romeo and Juliet (2026-10-20)

vocabulary.context:
Sir Paris, I will make a desperate tender
Of my child’s love: I think she will be ruled
In all respects by me; nay, more, I doubt it not.
vocabulary.source: Liber et Libri contextual definition, hand-written against the line in Romeo and Juliet (2026-10-20)

etymology.text: “desperate”: From Middle English desperat(e) "desperate", borrowed from Latin dēspērātus, perfect passive participle of dēspērō "to be without hope", see -ate. The noun is derived from the adjective or from the Latin source through substantivization, see -ate.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Capulet's decision reverses his earlier respect for Juliet's consent. Useful evidence: “Sir Paris, I will make a desperate tender / Of my child’s love” (Act III, Scene IV, Capulet (speech 4)): Capulet offers Juliet impulsively. Theme link: Capulet decides for Juliet without asking her. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
